The third season of the American [[sitcom]] ''[[The Office (American TV series)|The Office]]'' premiered in the United States on [[NBC]] on September 21, 2006, and concluded on May 17, 2007. The season had a total of 25 half-hours of material, divided into 16 half-hour episodes, five 40-minute "super-sized" episodes, and two one-hour episodes. ''The Office'' is an American adaptation of the [[The Office (British TV series)|British TV series]] as a [[mockumentary]] portraying the daily lives of office employees in the Scranton, Pennsylvania branch of the fictitious [[Dunder Mifflin|Dunder Mifflin Paper Company]]. The season stars [[Steve Carell]], [[Rainn Wilson]], [[John Krasinski]], [[Jenna Fischer]], and [[B. J. Novak]], with supporting performances from [[Melora Hardin]], [[David Denman]], [[Ed Helms]], [[Leslie David Baker]], [[Brian Baumgartner]], [[Kate Flannery]], [[Mindy Kaling]], [[Angela Kinsey]], [[Paul Lieberstein]], [[Oscar Nunez]], and [[Phyllis Smith]].

The season marked the move of main character [[Jim Halpert]] (John Krasinski) from [[Scranton, Pennsylvania|Scranton]] to [[Stamford, Connecticut|Stamford]], and also introduced [[Rashida Jones]] as [[Karen Filippelli (fictional character)|Karen Filippelli]], and Ed Helms as [[Andy Bernard]]—both members of Dunder Mifflin Stamford—as recurring characters. Helms would later be promoted to series regular. The main plot for the early episodes of the season deals with a recurring problem in seasons one and two—the problem of company downsizing—while in the last half of the season, intra-office relationships (specifically those among Pam, Jim, and Karen; Dwight and Angela; and Michael and [[Jan Levinson]]) also become major plot points.

The third season of ''The Office'' aired on Thursdays at 8:30&nbsp;p.m. ([[Eastern Time Zone|ET]]). The season saw its ratings increase from the previous. In addition, it continued the critical praise that had started during the show's second season. The season was released on DVD in a box set containing four discs. While the DVD features all 25 episodes, the episodes "[[Traveling Salesmen]]" and "[[The Return (The Office)|The Return]]" were condensed into one episode. The set contained commentaries from creators, writers, actors, and directors on some of the episodes, while also containing [[deleted scene]]s from all of the episodes. It was released by [[Universal Studios Home Entertainment]].

== Production ==

''The Office'' was officially renewed for a third season before the second-season episode "[[The Carpet (The Office)|The Carpet]]" aired on January 26, 2006. Series star [[Jenna Fischer]] noted that while it is rare "to hear news of a pickup so early", the decision came early because of how pleased [[NBC]] was with the show's burgeoning success.<ref name="tvguide" /> 

This season of the show was produced by [[Reveille Productions]] and Deedle-Dee Productions, both in association with [[NBC Universal Television Studio]]s. The show is based on the British series created by [[Ricky Gervais]] and [[Stephen Merchant]], who are [[executive producer]]s on the show and wrote the third-season episode "[[The Convict]]".<ref name="GreenLight">{{cite news|last=Wood|first=David|title=American Office Gets Green Light|url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2004/may/18/broadcasting.internationalnews|access-date=September 28, 2012|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|date=May 18, 2004}}</ref> This season was produced by [[Greg Daniels]], who also served as its [[showrunner]]. Returning writers included Daniels, [[Michael Schur]], [[Gene Stupnitsky]], [[Lee Eisenberg]], [[Jennifer Celotta]], [[Mindy Kaling]], [[Paul Lieberstein]], and [[B. J. Novak]]. New writers for the season included [[Brent Forrester]], [[Justin Spitzer]], and Caroline Williams.<ref name="DVD">{{cite AV media notes |title=The Office: The Complete Third Season |last=Kwapis |first=Ken Kwapis |type=DVD |publisher=[[NBC]] |display-authors=etal}}</ref>

This season's episodes were directed by twelve different directors: Of these individuals, Daniels, [[Ken Kwapis]], [[Ken Whittingham]], [[Randall Einhorn]], [[Tucker Gates]], [[Jeffrey Blitz]], and [[Harold Ramis]] all directed multiple episodes, whereas [[Roger Nygard]], [[Miguel Arteta]], [[Julian Farino]], [[Joss Whedon]], and [[J. J. Abrams]] each directed an episode apiece.<ref name="DVD" /><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://tv.ign.com/articles/754/754846p1.html |publisher=[[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]]|work=[[IGN]] |title=Joss Whedon and J.J. Abrams Both Directing The Office |date=January 11, 2007 |access-date=January 2, 2012}}</ref> Gordon, Kwapis, Whittingham, and Daniels had all previously directed episodes during [[The Office (American season 1)|seasons one]] and [[The Office (American season 2)|two]].<ref name="DVD" />  While ''The Office'' was mainly filmed on a studio set at Valley Center Studios in [[Van Nuys]], [[California]],<ref name="TheDundiesCommentary">"The Dundies" [Commentary track], ''The Office'' Season Two (US/NBC Version) [DVD], 2006, Los Angeles, CA: [[Universal Television|Universal]].</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Glassman |first=Thea |date=March 19, 2020 |title=How the Remarkably Unremarkable World of Dunder Mifflin Was Built |url=https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/the-office-anniversary-dunder-mifflin-set-design |access-date=January 6, 2025 |website=Architectural Digest |language=en-US}}</ref> the city of [[Scranton, Pennsylvania]], where the show is set, was used for shots of the opening theme.<ref>{{cite news|last=Marchese|first=John|title=Scranton Embraces the 'Office' Infamy|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/10/21/arts/television/21marc.html|access-date=September 28, 2012|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=October 21, 2007}}</ref> 

After reports that claimed the show would be "ending in March" were released, Fischer clarified in a [[TV Guide (magazine)|''TV Guide'']] article that this date referred only to the season finale and that the show had been renewed for another season.<ref name="tvguide">{{cite web |last=Fischer |first=Jenna |date=January 26, 2006 |title=The Office Presents: 'The Carpet' |url=http://www.tvguide.com/news/Office-Presents-Carpet-36178.aspx |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100313141436/https://www.tvguide.com/news/Office-Presents-Carpet-36178.aspx/ |archive-date=March 13, 2010 |access-date=October 4, 2012 |work=[[TV Guide]]}}</ref> However, this season's finale would eventually air in May, rather than March.<ref name="ewreview2">{{Cite magazine |last=West |first=Abby |date=May 20, 2007 |title=Corporate Madder |url=https://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20039421,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070520053010/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20039421,00.html |archive-date=May 20, 2007 |access-date=May 24, 2012 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]}}</ref>

== Cast ==
{{see also|List of The Office (American TV series) characters}}
[[File:Rashida Jones @ the 2007 Fox Television Upfronts.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Rashida Jones]] had a recurring role in the third season as [[Karen Filippelli (fictional character)|Karen Filippelli]].|alt=]]

''The Office'' employed an [[ensemble cast]]. Most of the main characters, and some supporting ones, are based on characters from the British version of the show. While these characters normally have the same attitudes and perceptions as their British counterparts, the roles have been redesigned to better fit the American show. The show featured a large cast size, many of whom were known for their [[Improvisation|improvisational]] work.<ref name="office-original">{{cite web |last1=Gilbert |first1=Holly |date=November 1, 2020 |title=The Office US Vs. UK Versions: Differences Explained |url=https://screenrant.com/office-us-vs-uk-versions-differences-explained/ |access-date=December 18, 2025 |website=[[Screen Rant]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Glassman |first=Thea |date=March 19, 2020 |title=How the Remarkably Unremarkable World of Dunder Mifflin Was Built |url=https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/the-office-anniversary-dunder-mifflin-set-design |access-date=January 6, 2025 |website=Architectural Digest |language=en-US}}</ref> 

===Main===
* [[Steve Carell]] as [[Michael Scott (The Office)|Michael Scott]], Regional Manager of the Dunder Mifflin Scranton Branch. Loosely based on [[David Brent]], Gervais' character in the British version,<ref>{{cite news|last=Stanley|first=Alessandra|title=Jolly Good Show Or Was It?; On TV, Attitude Is More Important Than the Way the Vowels Sound|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9800EFD81F30F93BA35757C0A9619C8B63&scp=20&sq=the+office+carell&st=nyt|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=September 28, 2012|date=April 8, 2007}}</ref> Scott is a dim-witted and lonely man, who attempts to win friends as the office comedian, usually making himself look bad in the process. 
* [[Rainn Wilson]] as [[Dwight Schrute]], who, based upon [[Gareth Keenan]], is the Assistant to the Regional Manager, although the character frequently fails to include "to the" in his title.<ref>{{cite news|last=Rooney|first=Brian|title=The Man Behind 'The Office's' Favorite Suck-Up, Dwight Schrute|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Nightline/story?id=3566414&page=1#.UGYDWGjd7ww|work=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|access-date=September 28, 2012|date=September 7, 2007}}</ref> 
* [[John Krasinski]] as [[Jim Halpert]], a sales representative and prankster, who is based upon [[Tim Canterbury]], and is in love with [[Pam Beesly]], the receptionist.<ref>{{cite news|last=Carter|first=Bill|title='The Office' Transfers to a New Cubicle|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/03/20/arts/television/20Cart.html|access-date=September 28, 2012|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=March 20, 2005}}</ref> 
* [[Jenna Fischer]] as [[Pam Beesly]], who is based on [[Dawn Tinsley]]. She is shy, but is often a cohort with Jim in his pranks on Dwight.<ref name=ny3>{{cite news|last=Alessandra|first=Stanley|title=An American-Style ''Office'' With a Boss From Heck|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/03/24/arts/television/24stan.html|access-date=September 28, 2012|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=March 24, 2005}}</ref> 
* [[B. J. Novak]] as [[Ryan Howard (The Office)|Ryan Howard]], who for the first two seasons is a [[temporary worker]], but is promoted to sales representative in this season.<ref name=ny3/>

===Starring===
* [[Melora Hardin]] as [[Jan Levinson]], Michael's boss and love interest.
* [[David Denman]] as Roy Anderson, Pam's ex-fiancé and a warehouse worker.
* [[Ed Helms]] as [[Andy Bernard]], a preppy salesman with anger issues, who is transferred from the Stamford branch.
* [[Leslie David Baker]] as Stanley Hudson, a grumpy salesman.
* [[Brian Baumgartner]] as [[Kevin Malone]], a dim-witted accountant.
* [[Kate Flannery]] as Meredith Palmer, a [[promiscuity|promiscuous]] supplier relations representative.
* [[Mindy Kaling]] as [[Kelly Kapoor]], the shallow and talkative customer service representative.
* [[Angela Kinsey]] as [[Angela Martin]], a judgemental accountant, who serves as Dwight's love interest.
* [[Paul Lieberstein]] as Toby Flenderson, the sad-eyed human resources representative.
* [[Oscar Nunez]] as [[Oscar Martinez (The Office)|Oscar Martinez]], an intelligent accountant, who is also gay.
* [[Phyllis Smith]] as Phyllis Vance, a motherly saleswoman.<ref name=tguidecast/>

===Recurring===
* [[Rashida Jones]] as Karen Filippelli, a saleswoman transferred from the Stamford branch, who serves as Jim's new love interest.
* [[Creed Bratton]] as Creed Bratton, the office's strange quality assurance officer.
* [[Craig Robinson (actor)|Craig Robinson]] as Darryl Philbin, the warehouse manager.
* [[Andy Buckley]] as [[David Wallace (The Office)|David Wallace]], Dunder Mifflin's CFO.
* [[Charles Esten]] as Josh Porter, Regional Manager of the Dunder Mifflin Stamford branch.<ref name=tguidecast>{{cite web|title=The Office Cast and Details|url=http://www.tvguide.com/tvshows/the-office/cast/191831|work=[[TV Guide]]|access-date=September 30, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120130215641/https://www.tvguide.com/tvshows/the-office/cast/191831/|archive-date=January 30, 2012}}</ref>

== Reception ==

===Ratings===
{{image frame
|content={{#chart:OfficeUS3ratings.chart}}
|width = 500
|caption = Ratings for each episode of ''The Office'' that aired this season.{{ref|cite|i}}
}}
The third-season premiere "[[Gay Witch Hunt]]" received a 5.7/9 in the [[Nielsen ratings]], meaning that on average 5.7 percent of households were tuned in at any given moment and 9 percent of all televisions in use at the time were tuned into the program.<ref name=gayratings/> The premiere was watched by 9.1 million viewers, and marked a slight increase from the [[The Office (American season 2)|second season]] premiere "[[The Dundies]]".<ref name=gayratings/><ref name="boysngirls-3" /> At the onset of the season, the show began to eclipse the viewership of its lead-in program, ''[[My Name Is Earl]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=ABC Changes 'Anatomy' of Thursday|url=http://www.zap2it.com/tv/ratings/zap-ratings092106,0,2646665.story?coll=zap-news-headlines|work=[[Zap2it]]|publisher=[[Tribune Media Services]]|access-date=December 19, 2012|date=September 22, 2006|archive-date=September 13, 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090913105605/http://www.zap2it.com/tv/ratings/zap-ratings092106,0,2646665.story?coll=zap-news-headlines|url-status=dead}}</ref> The season hit a low with the nineteenth episode "[[The Negotiation (The Office)|The Negotiation]]", which was viewed by 6.74 million viewers.<ref name="boysngirls-3" /> The season finale, "[[The Job (The Office)|The Job]]" was viewed by 7.88 million viewers, also an increase from the second-season finale "[[Casino Night]]".<ref name="boysngirls-3" /> By the end of the 2006–07 season, it placed 68th, a one-place slip from the previous season. Despite this, the show's third season was slightly more watched than the previous: it averaged 8.3 million viewers, and scored a 4.1/11 in the [[Nielsen ratings]], meaning that on average 4.1 percent of households 18–49 years old were tuned in at any given moment and 11 percent of all televisions in use at the time were tuned into the program. This season of ''The Office'' also ranked as the 28th-most watched series in the 18–49 demographic.<ref>{{cite web|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|publisher=[[Prometheus Global Media]]|url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/television/features/e3ifbfdd1bcb53266ad8d9a71cad261604f|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071025030515/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/television/features/e3ifbfdd1bcb53266ad8d9a71cad261604f|archive-date=October 25, 2007|title=2006–07 Primetime Wrap}}</ref>

===Reviews===
The third season of ''The Office'' was met with critical acclaim. Review aggregator website [[Metacritic]] gave the third season of the show an 85 out of 100 rating, which indicates "universal acclaim".<ref>{{cite web|title=The Office: Season 3|url=http://www.metacritic.com/tv/the-office/season-3|work=[[Metacritic]]|publisher=[[CBS Interactive]]|access-date=December 19, 2012}}</ref> Travis Fickett of [[IGN]] wrote that, in its third season, ''The Office'' was one of the "smartest, funniest and most likable shows" on television.<ref name=ign>{{cite web|last=Fickett|first=Travis|title=The Office: Season 3 Review|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2007/06/01/the-office-season-3-review|work=[[IGN]]|publisher=[[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]]|access-date=December 19, 2012|date=June 1, 2007}}</ref> ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' writer Meeta Agrawal praised the show for separating the action between Jim in Stamford and the rest of the characters in Scranton{{Em dash}}a creative choice, Agrawal argued, that many other shows would have likely fumbled.<ref name=ew/> Ultimately, Agrawal gave the season an "A−".<ref name=ew>Agrawal, Meeta (August 31, 2007). "[https://web.archive.org/web/20070903154525/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20054077,00.html The Office: Season 3]," ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''. Retrieved on January 27, 2008.</ref> Francis Rizzo III of [[DVD Talk]] called the season "an outstanding year for the Scranton crew" and praised the "unbelievably funny 21 episodes in between" the opener and the finale as reasons as to why it was "a great stand-alone season from easily one of the funniest shows on TV."<ref name=dvdtalk>{{cite web|last=Rizzo|first=Francis|title=The Office – Season Three|url=http://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/30182/office-season-three-the/|work=[[DVD Talk]]|publisher=[[Internet Brands]]|date=September 4, 2007}}</ref>

The third season was the first season to feature hour-long episodes, "[[A Benihana Christmas]]" and "[[The Job (The Office)|The Job]]".<ref name=commentary>{{cite AV media |people=[[Jenna Fischer|Fischer, Jenna]], [[Ken Kwapis]], [[Melora Hardin]], [[John Krasinski]], [[David Rogers (film editor)|David Rogers]] |date=2007 |title=Audio commentary for "The Job" | medium=DVD |publisher=[[Universal Studios Home Entertainment]] }} ''The Office: Season Three'' Disc 4</ref> While the [[The Office (American season 4)|following season]] would be criticized for its overuse of hour-long episodes, both of season three's longer episodes received a favorable reception.<ref>{{cite web|title=Please, NBC, Stop the Hour-long 'Office' Madness!|url=http://www.vulture.com/2007/10/please_nbc_stop_the_hourlong_o.html|work=[[New York (magazine)#Digital|Vulture]]|publisher=New York Media, LLC|access-date=December 19, 2012|date=October 18, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= http://tv.ign.com/articles/751/751316p1.html |title= The Office: "A Benihana Christmas" Review |access-date=July 10, 2008 |last= Goldman |first= Eric |date= December 15, 2006 |publisher=[[News Corporation (1980–2013)|News Corporation]]|work=[[IGN]]}}</ref><ref name=ewreview>{{Cite magazine |url=http://www.ew.com/recap/office-more-things-change |title=Corporate Madder |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |first=Abby |last=West |date=May 20, 2007 |access-date=May 24, 2012 |archive-date=May 17, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120517092217/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20039421,00.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Awards ===
The third season of ''The Office'' received seven nominations for [[Primetime Emmy Awards|Primetime Emmys]] at the [[59th Primetime Emmy Awards]], and won the award for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series for the episode "Gay Witch Hunt", as well as the award for Outstanding Single-camera Picture Editing For A Comedy Series for "The Job".<ref name=emmys>{{cite web|title=The Office|url=http://www.emmys.com/shows/office|work=Emmys.com|publisher=[[Academy of Television Arts & Sciences]]|access-date=December 20, 2012}}</ref> ''The Office'' was also nominated for the Emmy for Outstanding Comedy Series, with the award going to ''[[30 Rock]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Outstanding Comedy Series – 2007|url=http://www.emmys.com/award_history_search?person=&program=&start_year=2007&end_year=2007&network=All&web_category=363&winner=All|work=Emmys.com|publisher=[[Academy of Television Arts & Sciences]]|access-date=December 20, 2012}}</ref> Other nominations included Outstanding Lead Actor in a Comedy Series for Steve Carell for his portrayal of Michael Scott, Outstanding Supporting Actor for Rainn Wilson for his portrayal of Dwight Schrute, Outstanding Supporting Actress for Jenna Fischer for her portrayal of Pam Beesly, Outstanding Directing for a Comedy Series for Ken Kwapis for directing the episode "Gay Witch Hunt", and another nomination for Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series for [[Michael Schur]] for the episode "The Negotiation".<ref name=emmys/>

They wait outside all day, but David never shows up, and they resign themselves to defeat. However, Josh, the regional manager of the Stamford branch, announces that he is leaving the company to take another job, and a decision is made for the Scranton branch to absorb the Stamford branch instead. == DVD release ==
The third season of ''The Office'' was released by Universal Studios Home Entertainment as a four-disc Region 1 DVD box set on September 4, 2007, followed by a Region 2 release on July 21, 2008.<ref name=dvdtalk/><ref>{{cite web |title=''Office'' [US], ''The'' S3 DVD |url=https://limelightcollection.co.uk/products/office-us-the-s3-dvd |website=Lime Light |access-date=January 21, 2026}}</ref> The set contains all 25 episodes—including the "super-sized" and one-hour installments—presented in a 1.78:1 aspect ratio with Dolby Digital 5.1 Surround sound and optional English and Spanish subtitles. Bonus features include audio commentaries on 8 episodes, as well as an assortment of deleted scenes. The collection also features a variety of digital and promotional content, such as the "Kevin Cooks Stuff in the Office" featurette, the "Lazy Scranton" and Dwight Schrute music videos, an interview with Joss Whedon, a series of "Toby Wraparounds", a blooper reel, excerpts from the 2006 NBC Primetime Preview and the 58th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards, and winning entries from the "Make Your Own Promo" contest.<ref name="DVD"/>

== Explanatory notes ==
{{note|a|†}} denotes a "super-sized" 40-minute episode (with advertisements; actual runtime around 28 minutes).<br>
